terms.notes: Baseline vocabulary already used throughout plan generation (Roti, Dal, Curd, Sabzi, Paneer are North Indian/Hindi terms) — no renaming needed.

Too broad to give one glossary — overlaps Tamil, Telugu, Kerala-style and Karnataka, each covered separately below with its own distinct vocabulary. Prefer the specific region when the client named one.

Umbrella label for 7+ states and dozens of unrelated languages (Assamese, Manipuri, Naga, Khasi, Mizo, etc.) with no shared food vocabulary. A single glossary entry would be meaningless — needs a per-state/per-community breakdown if this region is ever prioritized.
Client's household follows a blend of regional cuisines — no single regional vocabulary applies. Falls back to default (North Indian/Hindi) naming.
Fulka/Phulka and Roti are used interchangeably in Punjab — this is a common alternate name, not a strict replacement; either is understood.
No distinct Punjabi word found — same as the default 'Dal'.
Dahi — same word as the Hindi default already in use.

In Punjab 'Lassi' commonly refers to a thicker, often sweetened yogurt drink — not always identical to plain thin buttermilk (chaas). Confirm with a dietitian before treating these as interchangeable.
Shared Hindi-belt term, not Punjabi-exclusive.
Ghee is a shared pan-Indian term — no distinct Punjabi word.
Rotli is thin wheat roti specifically. 'Rotla' is a different, thicker bajra-flour bread — a distinct food, not just a rename of wheat roti; do not conflate the two.
Confirmed same word 'Dal' used in Gujarati (e.g. 'Dal Bhaat', 'Gujarati Dal') — no distinct rename.
Dahi — same word as the Hindi default.
As in 'Dal-Bhaat-Rotli', the everyday Gujarati thali.

Same spelling/word as the Hindi default, listed for completeness.
Also called 'Mattha' locally.
Also spelled 'Tup'.
Essentially the Bengali pronunciation of 'Roti' for everyday flatbread. Bengali cuisine also has distinct fried breads (Luchi, Porota) that are different dishes, not renames of roti.
Bengali also just says 'Dal' — same word.
'Mishti doi' (sweet curd) is a distinct Bengali specialty dessert — not the same as everyday plain curd.
No distinct term surfaced after two search passes — needs a native-speaker check.

Same base word as the Hindi-belt term. Bengali distinguishes seasonal/form-specific specialty variants — 'Nolen Gur' (fresh winter date-palm jaggery), 'Patali Gur' (solid), 'Jhola Gur' (liquid) — these are specific dishes, not swaps for jaggery in general.
Ghee is a shared pan-Indian term.
Same word 'Roti' used — no distinct rename. 'Litti' (sattu-stuffed, baked) is a different, specific dish, not a general roti rename.
Same word as default.
Same as Hindi default; used in local dishes like 'Dahi Chuda'.
'Arwa rice' is a specific rice variety grown in Bihar/Jharkhand — a distinct food, not a general rename of 'rice'. Do not auto-substitute.
Shared Hindi-belt term (Bhojpuri/Magahi/Maithili are closely related to Hindi) — no distinct local word found.
Ghee is a shared pan-Indian term.

'Bajra roti'/'Bajre ki roti' (pearl-millet flatbread) is the everyday staple bread in Rajasthan/Marwar — a genuinely different grain, not a rename of wheat roti. 'Baati' (hard baked wheat bread) is also a distinct dish. Confirm the client's actual staple grain before substituting either.
Same word as default; named varieties (Tuvaar, Chana, Mung, Moth, Urad dal) use the same names as elsewhere.
Same as Hindi default.
Shared Hindi-belt term.
Also spelled 'Gud'. Shared Hindi-belt term.
Ghee is a shared pan-Indian term.
No reliable distinct term — Kerala cuisine is rice-centric with no strong native roti tradition.
Same Sanskrit root as Tamil 'Thayir'; Malayalam spelling/pronunciation is 'Thair'/'Tair'.
Choru is cooked rice specifically; 'Ari' is the raw grain — pick based on context.
No reliable distinct term — Tamil Nadu is rice-centric; 'chapati'/'parotta' are used as borrowed terms, not native Tamil words.
'Pasi paruppu' specifically means moong dal — only use that more specific term when the food actually is moong dal, not as a stand-in for dal in general.
Also spelled 'Moru'. 'Mor Kuzhambu' is a specific buttermilk-based curry, a different dish from plain buttermilk.
As in 'Nei Sadam' (ghee rice).
No distinct native term found — Telugu cuisine borrows 'Chapatti' directly, similar to Tamil.
'Mudda pappu' specifically means plain toor dal and 'Bellam pappu' means dal cooked with jaggery — dish-specific names, do not use them as a generic 'dal' swap.
Annam is cooked rice; 'Biyyamu' is the raw grain.

Specifically a sorghum(jowar)-flour flatbread, the North-Karnataka staple — a different grain from wheat roti, not simply a regional rename. ('Akki rotti' is the rice-flour version.) Confirm the client's actual staple grain before substituting.
As in 'Majjige huli' (curried buttermilk).

Also spelled Tchot/Tsot. Kashmiri breads are largely a bakery tradition (kandur waan) — often leavened or baked, culturally distinct from a home-rolled wheat roti. Confirm with the client before treating as a like-for-like rename.

No reliable term surfaced after two search passes. Kashmiri has noticeably thinner web coverage than the other regions here — a native-speaker check will likely be faster than further automated search.

Only 'sweet curd' in a festive-dish context and 'Yakhni' (a yogurt-based SAUCE for meat/vegetables, not plain curd itself) surfaced — do not use Yakhni here, it names a prepared dish, not the ingredient. Needs a native-speaker check.
No reliable term surfaced after two search passes — needs a native-speaker check.
Tomul refers to husked raw rice; 'Batta' is specifically cooked rice — pick based on context.

Also spelled 'Machchhi'.
'Salan' is shared North Indian/Pakistani-Punjabi vocabulary rather than exclusively Indian-Punjabi — usable, but confirm it reads naturally to the specific client before using it.
Sabzi/Sabji is the Punjabi/Hindi word itself — no rename.
Same word 'Paneer' used, but not a traditionally common ingredient in Gujarati home cooking — expect it to appear less often than in North Indian plans.
'Patra ni Machhi' (banana-leaf-steamed) is a different, specific dish, not this generic curry term.
Same word 'Paneer' used.

Still not independently confirmed after two search passes — a source that surfaced 'matthi' turned out to describe Malabar (Kerala) cuisine, not Maharashtrian. Needs a native-speaker check rather than more search.

Kalvan is the generic Marathi word for a non-vegetarian curry/gravy, most associated with fish, but not an exclusive 'fish curry' compound the way Bengali's Macher Jhol is — a person should confirm it reads correctly in context.

Do NOT use 'Chhena' here — Chhena is a moister, unpressed fresh cheese used for Bengali sweets (rasgulla, sandesh), a genuinely different ingredient from paneer, not a regional synonym for it. Bengali cooking uses paneer as its own word when it uses paneer at all.
'Maacher' is the possessive/adjectival form ('of fish'), as in 'Maacher Jhol'.
Literally 'fish gravy' — the everyday, thin-gravy fish curry. 'Machher Jhal' (spicier) and 'Machher Kalia' (richer gravy) are distinct, more specific styles, not the same dish.
Torkari is the generic word for a vegetable dish. Labra, Chorchori, Ghonto and Chanchra are distinct specific mixed-vegetable preparations — not interchangeable renames of a single vegetable dish.
Same word 'Paneer' used (e.g. 'Paneer Ki Sabzi').
Same as the Hindi default.
'Jhor' parallels Bengali 'Jhol' (thin gravy) — both regions border each other linguistically. Less universally used than the Bengali term; confirm before using in a client-facing plan.
Same word 'Sabzi' used (e.g. 'Besan Ki Sabzi').
Same word 'Paneer' used (e.g. 'Paneer Ki Sabzi').

Confirmed absence, not just under-researched: Rajasthan is largely desert/landlocked, and traditional Marwari cuisine follows Jain vegetarian principles — fish has no established place in the everyday vocabulary.
Same reasoning as 'Fish' above — not a category this cuisine names.
'Sabzi' and 'Shaak' are both used interchangeably — same as default, no rename needed.
No distinct term surfaced — paneer is not a traditional Kerala ingredient.
Also written 'Meen kari' — prepared in many regional styles, this is the generic term.

No single generic word — Kerala cooking distinguishes 'Thoran' (dry, with grated coconut) from 'Mezhukkupuratti' (simple stir-fry, no coconut). These are different dishes, not interchangeable; do not auto-substitute either for a generic 'sabzi'.
No Tamil word exists — paneer is not a traditional Tamil ingredient, stays 'paneer'.
'Kuzhambu' is the generic Tamil word for a tamarind-based gravy; also spelled 'Meen kulambu'.

Poriyal is specifically a dry stir-fry. 'Kootu' (lentil-vegetable stew) and 'Kadamba poriyal' (mixed vegetables) are different preparations — Poriyal is the common default, not a claim about the actual cooking method used.
Confirmed used in Andhra/Telugu cuisine (e.g. Andhra-style paneer dishes) but under the same word 'Paneer' — no distinct Telugu term exists.
'Pulusu' specifically means a tamarind-based gravy — this is the common Andhra/Telugu fish-curry style, not the only one.
No distinct term surfaced after two search passes — needs a native-speaker check.
'Meenu' is likely correct (shared root with Tamil/Telugu/Malayalam) but two search passes have not independently confirmed it — needs a native-speaker check before use, not more automated search.
No reliable term surfaced after two passes — 'Saaru'/'Sambar' returned by an earlier search are rasam/lentil-soup terms, not fish curry, and must not be used here.
Palya specifically means a dry sautéed/fried vegetable dish — a wet vegetable curry may use a different word (e.g. 'Gojju'). Palya is the common default.

Tsaman is Kashmiri fresh cottage cheese, similar to paneer, and is also the name of a specific curry dish made with it. Verify with a native speaker before treating it as a direct like-for-like substitute for generic 'Paneer'.

Still no single generic term after two passes — Kashmiri fish dishes are named specifically instead: 'Gaad t Tamatar' (tomato-based), 'Muji Gaad' (with radish), 'Gaade Rogan Josh' (in a Rogan Josh-style gravy). Pick a specific named dish if the client's actual preparation is known; do not invent a generic gloss.
Haakh specifically means leafy greens (a specific Kashmiri collard-green dish) — do not apply to non-leafy vegetable dishes (e.g. a root-vegetable or okra preparation).
